stories.title: Pressure mounts on HSE board to explain O'Connor sacking
stories.summary: Pressure is mounting on the board of the HSE to elaborate on the events leading to Anne O'Connor’s dismissal as Chief Executive after both the Taoiseach and Tánaiste called for more information to be provided. Micheál Martin and Simon Harris yesterday moved to distance themselves from the board’s decision to sack Ms O’Connor as CEO after she confirmed she is to initiate court action against the HSE for the "unlawful termination" of her employment. Ms O’Connor, who was in the role for less than nine months, may decide to start court proceedings against her former employer later today. The HSE may also seek to bring its dispute with Ms O’Connor to mediation, where a private out-of-court settlement could be agreed. However, a spokesperson for Ms O'Connor has said "no formal offer of mediation" has been received at this time. Either scenario leaves the HSE open to significant costs, which would ultimately be borne by the Exchequer and increase political pressure on the Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill.

stories.title: Why we fall for Black Friday scams - and what we can do about it
stories.summary: Analysis: Consumers are caught out by scams which use urgency triggers, confirmation bias and trust signals to create a false sense of security and scarcity Sarah stared at her phone in disbelief. The €899 she had transferred for her daughter's Christmas present - a much sought-after PlayStation 5 bundle that had been "reduced" to half price for Black Friday - was gone. The website, which had appeared at the top of her Google search as a sponsored ad, had vanished. Her WhatsApp conversation with the "customer service representative" who had been so helpful in processing her order now showed as an inactive account. The sick feeling in her stomach deepened as she realized she’d fallen for a scam, despite considering herself tech-savvy and usually cautious with online purchases. "But it looked so legitimate," Sarah would later tell the gardaí. "They had the exact model I’d been searching for weeks. The reviews were perfect. The customer service rep even sent me a video of them packaging similar orders. When they said they only had three bundles left at that price, I didn’t want to miss out…" Sarah’s story represents thousands of consumers caught in the web of sophisticated seasonal scams each year, evidenced by fraudsters stealing almost €100 million through frauds and scams in 2023, an increase of over 16% on 2022. With Black Friday and Christmas around the corner, it is important to highlight that these scams aren’t merely about trickery; they also exploit the way we make decisions, turning our instincts and biases against us. Consumers are routinely ensnared by scams that deploy strategies like urgency triggers, confirmation bias and trust signals to create a false sense of security and scarcity. Understanding how these tactics work is the first step toward outsmarting them. The scam starts by creating urgency, playing on our natural tendency to avoid missed opportunities. High-demand items, especially with limited availability or time-limited discounts, can trigger a strong impulse to act quickly. For example, phrases like "only available for the next two hours" or "just three left in stock" are crafted to spark what’s known as the "urgency effect," where scammers play on a consumer’s levels of anxiety to convince them that this fantastic and amazing (but ultimately ridiculous) deal must be acted upon immediately to override our typical sense of caution.

stories.title: Israeli judges question Netanyahu corruption charges
stories.summary: Judges in the long-running corruption trial of Israeli caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu handed his defence a major boost by recommending the prosecution drop one of the cases in which he is accused of bribery. The recommendations, which came as Israel's longest-serving prime minister fights for his political survival, were immediately cheered by Mr Netanyahu's right-wing allies who demanded the trial be brought to an end. Mr Netanyahu's main rival Gadi Eisenkot has been tasked with forming a government after inconclusive 27 October elections and if he is no longer prime minister, he would lose his leverage to avoid a potential jail sentence. During a hearing in Jerusalem regarding three corruption cases against Mr Netanyahu, judges recommended dropping one, reconsidering another and suggested resolving the third through an agreement, Israeli media reported. In Case 4000, in which Mr Netanyahu is accused of bribery, fraud and breach of trust, judges indicated there was little chance of a conviction. That case is considered to be the most serious Mr Netanyahu faces and concerns him allegedly offering regulatory favours for a telecoms company in exchange for favourable media coverage.

stories.title: WC play-off: Six key players in battle to reach Brazil
stories.summary: The Republic of Ireland are in camp for the most important window of Carla Ward's reign to date: a two-legged World Cup play-off final against Poland. The countries collided twice in the qualifiers last April, the Girls in Green prevailing on both occasions, but they are evenly matched. We’ve looked at six players who could play key roles over the course of both legs, but excluded the captains Katie McCabe and Ewa Pajor. Their influence is obvious; the world-class duo are both capable of stealing the show. The question is, which members of the supporting cast will lay the most effective platform? Confirmation on Monday that Chloe Mustaki has suffered another ACL injury was a blow to the Girls in Green. The Nottingham Forest player has been brilliant for Ward since coming back into the fold in June 2025 for the friendlies against the USA. Mustaki has great chemistry with McCabe (the pair are the only left-footers regularly named in Ward's squads), and her ability to relieve the Chelsea star of defensive responsibilities while feeding her quick ball has been a key feature of Ireland’s best displays this year. She will be missed. Jessie Stapleton looks likely to get the nod in a central defensive back three. Still only 21 years old, the Dubliner is a good reader of the game with the talent to punch passes into midfield. The main question mark will be around her ability to wrap around McCabe down that left wing to offer more width. One of the stars of Poland’s Under-17s European Championships glory back in 2013, 30-year-old Kamczyk is now her country’s most capped player. The AC Milan midfielder can operate centrally or drift out towards the left. She may not be prolific (though certainly capable of chipping in with a goal), but creatively Kamczyk is a major asset.

stories.title: How one photographer captured the golden age of Irish clubbing
stories.summary: Looking back at the 90s is generally done through rose-tinted, blurry glasses; you only remember the great gigs, the great meals, and, of course, the great clubs, writes Anthony Remedy. The atmosphere-less club and the Nightlink trek home on a rainy Thursday in January isn't something you tell kids about twenty years later... Saying that, all the nights were kinda important at the time, to you or to someone. A person could have met the love of their life on a half-empty dance floor, or the love of their evening for maybe 24 hours. The music was always important, now and then. Whether it was house, techno, drum and bass, or whatever, the music and the nightlife meant the world to many of us. Clearly, nearly all these memories of dark clubs, the queues in, packed (or empty) dance floors, DJs from home or abroad mixing perfectly on the most basic of setups. It's hard not to think of these times as the best of times: the mid-90s to the 2000s. When clubs were very high in the social conversation, it was all new and exciting. Back then, no one I knew ever brought a camera out. We thought those nights would last forever. Luckily, photographer Brendan Duffy was hired by promoters across the country to capture DJs, dancers, and the club party scene. He shot everything on film, mostly for magazines like Mixmag or Clubbing.com, but sometimes just for fun.

stories.title: U2 pay tribute to Dolly Parton at NFL halftime show
stories.summary: U2 paid tribute to the late Dolly Parton as they returned to the NFL halftime stage in California overnight, performing some of their biggest hits alongside a song from their new album. The Dublin band headlined the NFL's inaugural Thanksgiving Eve halftime show at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, during the game between the Los Angeles Rams and the Green Bay Packers. The performance, which was streamed live on Netflix, saw Bono sing alongside Parton’s recorded vocals on Torn, with images of the country music star projected on screens surrounding the stage. The duet, which features on U2’s new album Carnaval de Luz, was Parton’s final vocal recording before her death in August at the age of 80. "We loved she would consider working with us, but she got out of her sickbed and sang her last song," he said. Bono also spoke about Parton’s ability to bring people together across political and cultural divides, explaining that the song, which explores divisions within a family, had originated with the country music star herself.

stories.title: Things to do in Dublin this weekend (November 27-29)
stories.summary: From festive flea markets to family-friendly raves, there is plenty happening in Dublin this weekend. Every Sunday, from 11am - 5pm, the Market Bar on Fade Street will host a Christmas Market. Expect plenty of stalls ranging from vintage and Vinyl to crafts and jewellery. Free to enter. Alternative Dublin is hosting a Christmas Card Making workshop in This Must Be The Place on Saturday, 28 November from 3pm - 5pm. Attendees will make a selection of cards in under two hours, with an artist providing materials, tools and inspiration while listening to Christmas music and winning prizes. Tickets €20.28. 333 Festival is set to return to The Devlin in Ranelagh on Saturday, 28 November, for its third edition. The event brings together some of the people shaping Irish culture right now across music, food, film, art and nightlife, taking over three floors of The Devlin for one day. So far, David Holmes, Donal Dineen, Jess Murphy, Billy Scurry, B+, Dandilion, Emmy Shigeta, Hewan, Ricky Chong and Paudi Cronin have been announced. There will also be the Dublin premiere of B+’s film, alongside talks and installations from All We Have Are Days and The Space Between. Tickets from €43.87. Kilmacud Musical Society is hosting a two-hour variety show celebrating some of the greatest movie musicals of all time. From the streets of Annie and the razzle dazzle of Chicago to the outrageous world of The Rocky Horror Picture Show and the timeless fun of Grease, the event includes show-stopping numbers, familiar favourites, and plenty of surprises. Running from 24-28 November, tickets range from €20-€24. As part of the 16 Days of Activism to End Gender Based Violence, the National Museum of Ireland is hosting a special edition tour, spotlighting six garments from the Museum's Changing Ireland galleries. Visitors will explore the experiences of ordinary Irish women through decades of Irish history in the realms of marriage, work, social class and religious subjugation. This tour will include discussions of Magdalene Laundries, institutional abuses, resistance, social justice and self-determination. Free, guided tour.

stories.title: Eight months: What we know about the sacking of a HSE CEO
stories.summary: The sacking of Anne O'Connor as CEO of the Health Service Executive (HSE) after less than eight months in the job has triggered a leadership crisis in the health system and a growing political storm. Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill says the decision was taken wholly independent of her by the HSE Board. She also says she ensured the Tánaiste and Taoiseach were "aware there was an escalated performance process" ongoing from September. However, the Taoiseach subsequently told the Dáil yesterday, "I have never expressed any support for the decision [to sack Anne O'Connor], I do not have the full details." He called for the "full facts" to be made public. Ms O'Connor has hit out against what she says was a "profoundly flawed" and unfair process. She says she was never told her job was at risk until the HSE chairman Ciarán Devane gave her an ultimatum to resign or be fired on a Teams call at 7.30am on Saturday morning. So, what is known about how Anne O'Connor went from being the best candidate for one of the most difficult jobs in the public service, to being fired less than eight months later? stories.title: BBC iPlayer expansion may allow ads and rival content
stories.summary: Britain is advancing plans to open up BBC iPlayer to advertising and rival broadcasters, potentially paving the way for an overhaul of the streaming platform, according to two people with knowledge of the matter. The proposal would represent a significant expansion of iPlayer's role as a platform for BBC programmes, with one of the people saying the technology upgrade that would be required could cost tens of millions of pounds. The potential technology investment to allow iPlayer to carry advertising attached to content from rivals including Channel 4 has not been reported previously. It is part of wider efforts among British broadcasters to compete with global streaming services such as Netflix, Disney and Amazon Prime Video. The change is expected to feature in a White Paper on the BBC's charter renewal, due by the end of the year, setting out the UK government's position on the public broadcaster's funding, governance and remit from 2028, the two people said. The BBC pointed to comments by Director General Matt Brittin, who in July said one opportunity for Channel 4 would be "in partnership with the BBC, having content on iPlayer, but continuing to be ad-funded".

stories.title: Dublin church unveils stained-glass AIDS memorial windows
stories.summary: Two stained-glass windows commemorating people who died during the worldwide Aids epidemic and those who cared for them have been installed at St Teresa's Church in Dublin 8. The windows, at the Donore Avenue church, have been unveiled during its centenary year, ahead of World AIDS Day on 1 December. The parish said the memorials were intended to remember "all those who died of Aids, all those in Church and State who cared for them and all family and friends who grieve the great loss of loved ones". The windows were funded by a parish benefactor and constructed by Capital Glass of Leonard’s Corner. The first window features the red rose of St Teresa, a depiction of the Holy Spirit, images of people of different ages and backgrounds, and red Aids ribbons representing advocacy, research, fundraising and visibility. A rainbow is also incorporated into the design, while an alphabet along the bottom allows visitors to spell the names of people they have lost.

stories.title: Emma Fogarty, Colin Farrell, and The Slightest Touch
stories.summary: Some people will now say that Colin Farrell's best film is the one he stars in as himself. This winning documentary tells the story of epidermolysis bullosa (EB) campaigner Emma Fogarty's friendship with Farrell and their countdown to the 2024 Dublin City Marathon. By reaching the age of 40 in 2024, Fogarty had become the oldest person in Ireland with EB - the rare condition that causes blistering skin. It's no spoiler to say that Farrell ran the marathon and Fogarty joined him in a modified wheelchair for the last four kilometres, each representing a decade of her life. In the process, they raised over €1m for the EB charity DEBRA Ireland. Although their achievement has been well publicised, it doesn't diminish the power of The Slightest Touch, which effortlessly moves from joy to sadness and back again under the expert stewardship of director Rachel Fleit. Fleit contended, and Farrell acknowledged, that to make the documentary work, he would also have to open up his world to the cameras. And so, a man who says that he has "no interest in anyone knowing anything about my life" is interviewed in the California home he shares with his eldest son, James, who has the neurogenetic disorder Angelman syndrome, and youngest son Henry. This is Farrell at his most candid as he discusses hopes, fears, and hard-learned wisdom. "The reason I'm here is the reason you're here," he tells Fleit. "It's for Emma."

stories.title: PAC to question RTÉ executives over recruitment decisions
stories.summary: Sinn Féin TD John Brady, who is chair of the committee, said that he wanted "clear answers" on how the decisions were made and how they assisted the broadcaster in delivering its long-term strategy. Today's hearing was called after Minister for Communications and Media Patrick O'Donovan withheld €20 million from the broadcaster's 2027 funding over his dissatisfaction with the pace of reform. However, Director General Kevin Bakhurst will highlight progress, including cutting headcount by 98 over two years and completions under the first voluntary exit scheme. Ahead of the meeting, Mr Brady said the PAC wanted to get to the bottom of what exactly happened and why the decision was made to withhold the €20m. "While a number of bodies had responsibilities in this area, and separate strategy and reform documents were produced, there appears to have been no single, coherent framework linking the delivery of agreed reforms directly to the release and continuation of public funding. "The entire arrangement appears to have been characterised by fragmented oversight and a lack of clear accountability.

stories.title: Norse Atlantic suspends flights, warns of bankruptcy
stories.summary: Norwegian airline Norse Atlantic has suspended its flights today and said its board intends to file for bankruptcy if a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently. A day earlier, the long-haul budget carrier had warned that its financial situation was "critical" and that it required new financing for its short-term liquidity needs and operations, an announcement that sent its share price down 85%. "If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the Board's intention to file for bankruptcy," Norse said in a statement today. Norse continues to consider options to secure short-term financing and is in discussion with investors regarding a possible takeover that would include a financing solution, it said. "There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found," Norse added. European jet fuel costs more than doubled in March following supply disruptions linked to the US-Israeli war with Iran and have remained volatile at elevated levels through the year, hampering airlines.

stories.title: NFL: Rams take spoils in first Thanksgiving Eve game
stories.summary: The Los Angeles Rams beat the Green Bay Packers 26-13 in the NFL's first Thanksgiving-eve game. It was a high-stakes game for both teams as they vied for the final NFC wild-card spot. Running backs Blake Corum and Kyren Williams both scored touchdowns as the Rams secured their fifth straight win. The teams were tied 13-13 at half-time, but it was the Rams who came out firing in the third quarter and held the Packers scoreless in the second half. Packers quarterback Jordan Love threw for 198 yards and a touchdown, but was intercepted twice as Green Bay slumped to their second successive defeat. Rams safety Kamren Kinchens was ejected from the game for his illegal hit on the Packers' Christian Watson shortly before half-time.

stories.title: Around 40 jobs to go as HSI set to be liquidated
stories.summary: Horse Sport Ireland, the country's governing body for equestrian sport, is set to be liquidated, with the loss of around 40 jobs. A High Court hearing is scheduled for this morning, during which the company's liquidation is expected to be confirmed. The organisation entered examinership in August as it was unable to pay its debts. At the time, HSI - which is heavily reliant on State funding - said this followed a substantial liability relating to the defence of a longstanding legal action. An examiner had proposed a rescue plan for HSI, but this plan was not accepted by stakeholders. While not confirming the liquidation, a spokesperson for the Department of Agriculture said it has been "engaging with the examiner extensively throughout ... on all legal and operational issues throughout this entire process".

stories.title: Pochettino 'so proud' of players after draw in Lisbon
stories.summary: Mauricio Pochettino was proud of Manchester United's performance and his players’ early progress in the action-packed 2-2 draw at Sporting Lisbon in the Champions League. The former Argentina international began his reign with a chastening 4-0 loss at rivals Liverpool on Sunday, when Leny Yoro’s early – and subsequently overturned – red card was the catalyst for Anfield agony. More frustration followed on Wednesday, when Senne Lammens gifted Sporting a penalty converted by Luis Suarez shortly after denying him from the spot before Bruno Fernandes’ double with the help of a bobble put United in front. But Suarez would level in the second half after nudging Lammens when attempting to gather a high ball and Pochettino’s hopes of a first win ended when home goalkeeper Kaique Pereira’s own goal was ruled out. Szymon Marciniak adjudged Patrick Dorgu to have fouled him having been sent to the monitor on a night when the referee’s early whistle meant a disallowed first half Amad Diallo goal could not be overturned. Youri Tielemans was incorrectly booked for his role in that incident and picked up a second booking at the end of an eventful night that saw Pochettino focus on the positives in Portugal.

stories.title: Nepal moves to declare dead those missing after floods
stories.summary: Nepal has begun a process to legally declare dead thousands of people still missing after its catastrophic summer floods, authorities have said, three months after the disaster. A high-altitude glacier on the Nepal-China border collapsed on 26 August, unleashing a torrent of water, ice, rock and debris. In Nepal, the floods killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,500 missing. Among the missing were two Irish citizens - 46-year-old Santosh Sahu and 18-year-old Spandan Sahu – who had been on a tour. "We have started the process to declare the missing dead by verifying their details," Ram Bahadur KC, spokesman for the disaster management authority, said. Authorities have issued public notices naming about 4,000 missing people, including 623 foreign nationals, and asked for objections or corrections before formal declarations are made.

stories.title: Farrell confirms Crowley returned to Irish camp last week
stories.summary: Jack Crowley spent time in Ireland camp last week as he continues to recover from a long-term vascular injury. Crowley last played when lining out for Munster in April. After a lengthy period ascertaining why he was unable to play, the Munster outhalf was diagnosed with rare lower-limb vascular injury involving a narrowing of a blood vessel. After ending the last Six Nations as Ireland's starting 10, he missed the end of the campaign with Munster as well as a pair of Nations Championship windows in July and November. Crowley is hoping to return to action during Munster’s Christmas/New Year fixtures, meaning he could be fit for next year’s Six Nations barring any setbacks. "He's doing okay," said Ireland head coach Andy Farrell. "He’s okay. He was in camp last week, which is great to see, him in good spirits. "He has started back with a bit of gradual return stuff, so I think it's just a bit of seeing how that progresses.

stories.title: Rare disease patients cite staffing for drug access delay
stories.summary: Patients with Spinal Muscular Atrophy say they are unable to access an approved drug for the rare condition due to staffing shortages at the main treatment centre. Dr Aoife McNicholl, an assistant professor in DCU, is one of around 75 people in Ireland with Spinal Muscular Atrophy - a neuromuscular disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness. She says the first treatment here for adults with the condition - a drug called Risdiplam - could be life-changing. The HSE Senior Leadership Team agreed to reimburse Risdiplam in August. Patients have to be assessed by a physiotherapist to see if they are eligible for the drug. But Dr McNicholl and others like her are still waiting to be seen at Beaumont Hospital's neuromuscular clinic. They say this is due to a shortage of dedicated physiotherapists there.

stories.title: McKibbin five off the lead in Australia
stories.summary: An opening round 69 sees Tom McKibbin five shots off the lead at the Australian PGA Championship where Haydn Barron sits top of the standings on eight-under-par. The Australian has given home supporters plenty to cheer about at the Lakes Club, with the world No 560 making nine birdies and dropping just one shot to open a two-shot lead over New Zealand's Kazuma Kobori. The 30-year-old plies his trade on the DP World Tour's secondary Hotel Planner Tour. McKibbin finished his round well in the opening event of the 2027 DP World Tour to sit on three-under-par. The only blot on the front nine was a bogey at the par-4 sixth, but that was sandwiched by birdies at the fourth and ninth. He dropped another at the 10th, but from there on in it was only positive, with birdies at 11, 13 and 17.

stories.title: Trump, NATO chief urge Russia not to 'expand' Ukraine war
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte urged Russia not to "expand the war" in Ukraine, in a joint statement issued after meeting in Florida. The "outstanding" and "very impactful" meeting focused on the wars in Ukraine and Iran, said the statement issued by the White House after the closed-door talks at Mr Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort. "We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible," the statement added. The joint appeal by Mr Trump and Mr Rutte comes despite the US leader describing Russian President Vladimir Putin as "my friend" during a meeting in China last week. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has taken issue with Mr Trump's comments on the Russian leader. Mr Rutte was asked about Mr Trump's comments in an interview with Fox News' "Fox & Friends".

stories.title: Ireland men's cricket team set for first tour of Pakistan
stories.summary: Ireland's men’s cricket team will make a first-ever visit to Pakistan for six 50-over matches as part of their preparations for the crucial ICC World Cup qualifier in February 2027. The match schedule will be from 13-24 January 2027, with the Irish squad arriving in Pakistan on 9 January. stories.title: Anthropic CEO denies wanting humans to give AI free will
stories.summary: Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei has denied wanting humanity to give up its free will to AI, calling it "absurd" to attribute the idea to him as rival tech leaders push back. "No, I do not believe that we should 'surrender human free will' to AI systems, and it's absurd to suggest that I do," Mr Amodei wrote in a lengthy post on X, a week after Anthropic's record-setting stock market debut. "We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security," he added. Fears that AI tools could slip out of human control have haunted Silicon Valley since a string of incidents this summer, including the hacking of Hugging Face by autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI. "We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!" an Anthropic safety lead, Evan Hubinger, wrote in September. Mr Amodei took aim, without naming names, at "some AI CEOs" who repeat slogans like "AI should be just a tool" but then are not "actually doing anything different in their products."

stories.summary: Following an impressive display in the Club Orange FAI Cup final, 30-year-old centre-back Patrick McClean has been named the SSE Airtricity/Soccer Writers Ireland Player of the Month for November. The younger brother of Irish centurion James McClean, the Creggan man capped a marvellous month with victory over Waterford in the decider at the Aviva Stadium to put a gloss on the Candystripes season. McClean was man of the match in the semi-final win over John Caulfield's Galway United but reserved his best performance of the season for the big day in the capital as Derry beat the Blues 1-0. The ex-Waterford, Glentoran and Sligo Rovers defender has just signed a contract extension at the Ryan McBride Brandywell. "It’s been a brilliant end to the year for us and the general feeling is that we will be better equipped to challenge for silverware again next season," he said. "I must say Mark Connolly did a massive job in getting us to the final and going on to win it. He took the handbrake off and allowed us play with freedom and it certainly showed in our performances. It was almost like we were two different teams.

stories.title: Humans may have been in Ireland earlier than records show
stories.summary: New excavations in a Waterford cave and a fresh examination of animal bones from the late 1800s found in the same area may show that humans lived in Ireland nearly 1,000 years earlier than currently confirmed, according to a study. The earliest evidence for people being in Ireland prior to the Mesolithic period is a butchered brown bear bone from Alice and Gwendoline Cave in Co Clare. However, findings in a new study show hunter gatherers may have lived in southern Ireland nearly a millennium earlier than currently confirmed. The study, published in the Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy, involved re-examining animal bones originally dug from Ballynamintra Cave in Waterford in 1878-1882 alongside analysing objects found in new excavations of the cave. Re-examining the National Museum of Ireland's 19th-century Ballynamintra Cave collection, the researchers identified two extinct giant deer leg bones bearing marks consistent with human butchery while the bones were still fresh. The study said a giant deer upper foreleg bone showed "a uniform chopping plane consistent with a heavy bladed stone tool used to hack the elbow joint apart".

stories.title: Myanmar opposes 'inappropriate' parts of genocide ruling
stories.summary: Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing has said that his government will not comply with "inappropriate" aspects of a United Nations' court ruling that the state committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, according to state media. Last week, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) delivered the verdict, finding that the country's forces systematically killed, raped and destroyed property of civilians from the mostly Muslim Rohingya during a 2017 crackdown in western Rakhine state. It ordered Myanmar authorities to prosecute and punish anyone suspected of perpetrating genocide, compensate survivors and facilitate safe passage home for refugees - more than 700,000 of whom fled to Bangladesh. The president Min said: "Myanmar would take the actions appropriate for a responsible country but would not comply with requirements it considered inappropriate." The ex-general commanded the military during the Rohingya crackdown before ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering an ongoing civil war. He was installed this year as civilian president following deeply restricted elections.

stories.title: Taoiseach to meet EU leaders on next long-term EU budget
stories.summary: Taoiseach Micheál Martin will join other EU leaders for a special summit in Brussels this morning aimed at closing the gap in negotiations on the next long-term EU budget. There are still sharp disagreements between richer member states and net beneficiary countries over the size and scope of the budget that will run from 2028 to 2034. Getting agreement on the budget has been the central challenge of the Irish EU presidency. The European Commission initially proposed a €2trn seven-year budget last year, and by the time the Irish Government took over the file, there were acute gaps between countries that want a bigger budget that focuses on agriculture and cohesion spending, and those wanting a smaller budget focused on competitiveness and defence spending. The Irish Government's long-awaited draft in October cut the original budget by 8% but seemed to leave neither the so-called frugal member states or the so-called friends of cohesion happy. The task was then taken up by President of the European Council António Costa, who chairs the regular gatherings of EU leaders.

stories.title: Stockdale and Timoney come in for Wallabies clash
stories.summary: Jacob Stockdale and Nick Timoney will start for Ireland in Friday's final Nations Championship clash with Australia, while Tadhg Beirne will take over captaincy in the absence of the suspended Dan Sheehan. Sheehan misses out after picking up a two-game ban following a croc roll in Saturday's 20-17 win against South Africa, with Timoney replacing him at the back of the Irish scrum. The only other change to the side that started last week's win against the Springboks is on the left wing, where Jacob Stockdale comes in for the injured Mack Hansen, with the Ulsterman making his first appearance of the November campaign. Head coach Andy Farrell has resisted making considerable changes to his side for the final game of 2026, with the two alterations being the fewest made between games since the start of 2025. It's the same starting front row for the third game in a row, with Rónan Kelleher packing down at hooker between Andrew Porter and Tadhg Furlong. Tadhg Beirne leads Ireland out for the third time as captain, and is joined in the second row by Joe McCarthy.
